source.title: Catalogue, Machine Age Exposition
source.creator: Fernand Léger, cover designer; New York City
source.preparation: Public-record packet manually prepared from Wolfsonian sources while automated API connectivity remains under investigation.

archivist.observation: The public checklist records a 1927 Machine Age Exposition catalogue with Léger cover design, dimensions, accession XM1999.108.8, and collection credit.
archivist.claim: This is a document about how machines were taught as culture; the packet supports bibliographic identity more than a full contents analysis.

evidence.text: Catalogue, Machine Age Exposition, 1927; Léger cover; XM1999.108.8
Checklist notes essays and an overview of European and American architecture and art

archivist.uncertainty: Full essay texts, exhibition checklist internals, and condition notes are not reproduced in this packet.
archivist.onsiteQuestion: What annotations, ownership marks, paper quality, or inserted ephemera appear only when the catalogue is handled as a library object?

worker.observation: The exposition placed machines, parts, photographs, and art in one pedagogical space; the catalogue is the portable script of that juxtaposition.
worker.claim: Mechanical beauty was not only aesthetic theory—it was a curriculum that trained eyes to admire industrial force and form.

evidence.text: Checklist describes embracing industrial technology's visual language in art, design, and architecture
Object is a catalogue (library material), not a machine itself

worker.uncertainty: Laborers who built the exhibited machines are not named in the short public description.
worker.onsiteQuestion: Which plates or captions in the physical catalogue make labor visible, and which aestheticize machinery into pure form?

futurist.observation: Léger's cover translates mechanical parts into geometry, aligning painting with industrial modernity.
futurist.claim: The catalogue argues that the machine age supplies a new formal language capable of organizing modern life—an early manifesto for technological aesthetics.

evidence.text: Cover designer Fernand Léger; 1927 New York exposition
Checklist links the show to streamlined forms and mechanical beauty

futurist.uncertainty: Whether visitors accepted that manifesto cannot be read from accession metadata alone.
futurist.onsiteQuestion: Does the physical sequence of images still feel like a forward program, or does it read as a dated ideology of progress?

mourner.observation: Celebrating the machine as beautiful can displace the bodies and risks attached to industrial systems.
mourner.claim: The catalogue's elegance may be a veil: admiration without account of injury, extraction, or coercion that machines also organized.

evidence.text: Public text emphasizes modernist ideas and mechanical beauty
Date places the document in interwar industrial culture

mourner.uncertainty: Critical social history is an interpretive lens; it is not printed as a field in the accession note.
mourner.onsiteQuestion: Where in the volume—if anywhere—do war technologies, workplace danger, or unequal modernization appear beside aesthetic praise?

propagandist.observation: An exposition catalogue is a rhetorical instrument: it selects, sequences, and legitimates what counts as the Machine Age.
propagandist.claim: Léger's cover and the essays teach allegiance to industrial modernity as taste, not only as fact.

evidence.text: Checklist states the exposition discussed modernist ideas and mechanical beauty
Cover attributed to a major modernist painter

propagandist.uncertainty: Publisher Jane Heap's organizing politics are only lightly implied by secondary descriptions, not fully present here.
propagandist.onsiteQuestion: How does the catalogue's typography, image hierarchy, and essay order persuade a reader to accept machines as cultural destiny?

counterfeit.observation: From the cover geometry one can invent a unified international consensus that art and industry had already reconciled.
counterfeit.claim: Every contributor agreed that mechanical form abolished political conflict—an unsupported synthesis labeled here as fabrication.

evidence.text: Packet does not include full essay texts or attendee testimony proving consensus

counterfeit.uncertainty: Intentionally unsupported: a tidy ending that real catalogues rarely provide.
counterfeit.onsiteQuestion: Which fluent totalizations about the Machine Age should stay quarantined until the pages and institutional context can contradict them?
